query: OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI and agents as of 2026 (gen_ai.* attributes, gen_ai.operation.name values such as invoke_agent / execute_tool / chat, gen_ai.agent.id, token usage attributes, error.type): status (experimental/stable), and how to model a multi-agent orchestration run (run → work item → agent invocation → tool call) with spans or events, plus CloudEvents for an append-only event journal. What should a small stdlib-only Python tool emit so it can later export to OTel without a dependency in the core?

content.text:
Use a versioned, append-only CloudEvents journal as your core contract, and derive OTel spans, logs, and metrics in an optional adapter. The relevant GenAI conventions remain Development, not Stable; error.type is a shared Stable attribute. Model durations as spans and state transitions as events—do not make the trace your durable workflow database.
One qualification on “as of 2026”: the official sources below are rolling documentation and repository main, checked for this answer, not an immutable October 13 release snapshot. Pin an actual GenAI semconv commit in your adapter before claiming compatibility.

## 1. Status and vocabulary

The main OpenTelemetry semantic-conventions documentation currently identifies itself as version 1.44.0 and says GenAI conventions have moved to the dedicated open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai repository. “Moved” in the old registry is not a stability designation. The dedicated inference and agent definitions explicitly mark the relevant GenAI spans and attributes Development.
“Experimental” is a reasonable informal description, but use the official label Development in your compatibility documentation.

## Operation names are semantic, not arbitrary phase labels

Do not invent gen_ai.operation.name="work_item" just because your scheduler has work items. Use a generic span with your own namespaced attributes unless that work item genuinely represents a defined GenAI operation.

## Identity distinctions that matter

- gen_ai.agent.id denotes a stable agent identifier. For hosted agents, use the provider-assigned resource identifier; the specification discourages transient in-memory instance IDs.
- Keep run_id, work_item_id, invocation_id, attempt_id, and worker/process IDs in your own schema. They answer different questions.
- gen_ai.conversation.id is a real conversation/session/thread identifier when available. Do not substitute a trace ID, generated UUID, or prompt hash merely to populate the field.
- Populate gen_ai.request.model on an agent span only when the agent is configured for a single model. For dynamic/multi-model agents, put model identity on the individual inference spans.
- Use gen_ai.provider.name, not deprecated gen_ai.system; use input/output token names, not deprecated prompt/completion token names.

## 2. Recommended trace model

For a bounded orchestration execution, I would use this tree:
```
invoke_workflow coding_pipeline INTERNAL ├── work_item implement INTERNAL, application-defined │ ├── invoke_agent implementer INTERNAL │ │ ├── chat <requested-model> CLIENT │ │ ├── execute_tool read_file INTERNAL │ │ ├── execute_tool apply_patch INTERNAL │ │ └── chat <requested-model> CLIENT │ └── invoke_agent reviewer INTERNAL │ ├── chat <requested-model> CLIENT │ └── execute_tool run_tests INTERNAL └── work_item integrate INTERNAL, application-defined
```
The agent conventions distinguish same-process invoke_agent spans (INTERNAL) from remote hosted-agent invocation spans (CLIENT). Inference spans are normally CLIENT, with INTERNAL allowed for same-process models. The official observability example likewise places chat and execute_tool under invoke_agent.
The application-defined work-item layer is my recommendation, not an OTel GenAI requirement.

## Tool calls and model calls are usually siblings

A model response can request a tool; the framework executes it after that inference operation finishes. Consequently, a tool execution is normally a child of the agent invocation, not a child of the already-completed model-call span.
Preserve the relationship using:
- gen_ai.tool.call.id, when available from the model/provider;
- your own causation_event_id;
- an optional span link to the inference that requested the tool.
The standard tool vocabulary includes gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type, and opt-in arguments/results.
Do not create a tool-execution span for a tool request that was denied or never executed. Journal the request and denial as facts instead.

## Spans versus events

My suggested mapping:
Do not force a DAG into a tree by choosing an arbitrary parent and losing the other dependencies. Store causality in the journal; use the trace tree for execution ownership.

## Retries and long-running runs

The GenAI inference convention says a logical operation span should include automatically retried requests and their elapsed duration. That is distinct from rerunning an entire agent invocation after a scheduler-level failure.
For your orchestrator, I recommend:
- one logical inference span around SDK-level retries;
- optional lower-level request spans/events for individual transport attempts;
- a new invocation/attempt span for each scheduler-level agent retry;
- separate trace segments across long suspension/resumption periods, correlated by stable run_id and explicit links.
A single trace for a short run is convenient. A single open span spanning days, approvals, crashes, and restarts is not a useful core persistence model. Keep total run elapsed time and active
